title: Convergence groups
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: Groups of homeomorphisms of a compact metric space in which every sequence of distinct elements has a subsequence collapsing the space, off one point, to another point. The first lesson proves from the definition by sequences that every element is elliptic, parabolic or loxodromic, describes the dynamics of loxodromic and parabolic elements, and shows that the stabilizer of a fixed point of a loxodromic element is virtually infinite cyclic. The second lesson shows that convergence actions and minimal actions pass to equivariant quotients, and that a convergence group on a compact connected metric space acts as a convergence group on the dendrite quotient of the space. The third lesson attaches to every point of the completion of an invariant set of cut points a closed connected subset of the space, its support, and proves that a minimal action fixes no point of the completion and that a parabolic element whose fixed point is not one of the chosen cut points fixes exactly one point of the completion. The fourth lesson determines the points of the completion fixed by a loxodromic element: at most three points next to each other, or exactly two points without neighbours, far apart, whose supports are the two fixed points of the element. The fifth lesson treats group actions on trees in the language of pretrees, contraction of edges, and the first identification on the completion: for a group with the fixed-point property for trees with finite edge stabilizers, no class of the finite interval relation of the completion is invariant. The sixth lesson proves, by transfinite induction along the construction of the dense quotient, that such a group fixes no point of the dendrite quotient, so that the dendrite quotient has more than one point, when the group is finitely generated, has the fixed-point property for trees, and has elements of infinite order in every infinite subgroup. The same induction shows that a group with these three properties which fixes a point of the dendrite quotient, for example when the quotient is a single point, fixes a point of the completion or preserves a class of its finite interval relation. The seventh lesson treats the case in which the group fixes a point of the dendrite quotient: then every cut point is fixed by a parabolic element, and the cut points are vertices of a tree with an action without inversions, finitely many orbits, no proper invariant subtree and infinite edge stabilizers, in which separation in the space is read off from paths. These are the facts about convergence groups used in OpenAI's proof (2026) of the Singer conjecture in dimension four outside the middle degree.
prerequisites: core course Point-Set Topology (C90): compact metric spaces
from the second lesson on: the course Pretrees (cut points of a connected space, the completion, the dendrite quotient of a continuum)
for the sixth lesson: ordinal numbers and transfinite induction (core course Mathematical Logic, Set Theory, and Computability), through the lesson The dense quotient of a pretree
the course proves every other fact it uses

checks.reading: Each proof was written out and re-read step by step on 11 Oct 2026; statements compared with Section 6 of Bowditch's memoir (author's version, library copy free/authors/bowditch/bhb-treelike.pdf), whose proofs use the action on distinct triples; here every proof uses collapsing sequences. Lesson 2 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Lemma 6.5 of the memoir and its remarks on naturality (pages 52, 56); the proofs use collapsing sequences; the statement on fixed points in a quotient (Corollary 1.2) and the equivariance of every step of the dendrite quotient are proved in the lesson. Lesson 3 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Lemmas 6.8, 6.10 and 6.11 of the memoir (pages 58-61); every step was re-derived. The statement that two supports meet in at most one point of T, which the memoir asserts without proof, is proved (Proposition 1.3). Lesson 4 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Lemma 6.9 of the memoir (pages 59-60); every step was re-derived. Spelled out beyond the memoir: why a connected invariant support with two points contains both fixed points; the exclusion of a third fixed point when an interval is infinite; the connectedness of the auxiliary sets N(p); and the reading of the memoir's 'N(p) = {p}' when p is not a point of T (the one point of N(p) is then a point of T adjacent to p, which contradicts that p has no neighbour). Lesson 5 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Lemmas 6.7 and 6.12 of the memoir (pages 58, 61); every step was re-derived. The memoir proves Lemma 6.7 by modifying a graph-of-groups argument; the lesson derives it from the fixed-point property by contracting the edges with infinite stabilizers (Propositions 2.1, 2.2). The fixed-point property itself (the memoir's Lemma 6.6 for one-ended groups) is a hypothesis in the lesson. Lesson 6 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Lemma 6.13 and the proof of Theorem 6.1 of the memoir (pages 61-63); every step was re-derived. The lesson adds the hypothesis that infinite subgroups contain elements of infinite order: the memoir's proof takes an element of infinite order in an infinite edge stabilizer without argument, so its Theorem 6.1 is not proved there for groups with infinite torsion subgroups, and the course does not prove that case. Two steps are repaired: in Lemma 6.13 the comparison with the median, and in the successor step the point through which the limit of the invariant arc is seen to lie in W. Lesson 6 was extended on 12 Oct 2026, 01:45 UTC: the induction is stated separately (Theorem 1.3) without the condition on the stabilizers of the cut points, which is needed only for the first two relations; an element of infinite order fixing two points of the completion at infinite distance is shown to be loxodromic without that condition (Lemma 3.2). Lesson 7 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Section 6 of OpenAI's manuscript 'The Singer conjecture in dimension four' (lemmas pret:parabolic-cuts, pret:invariant-class, proposition pret:tree); every step was re-derived. The manuscript obtains 'the dendrite quotient is a point' from Bowditch, Connectedness properties of limit sets, Lemma 1.4, which is not in the programme; the lesson takes its consequence as hypothesis (z). The statement that all edge stabilizers are infinite is derived from the fixed-point property for trees by contracting the other edge orbits, where the manuscript uses the structure theory of groups acting on trees.

open_obligations: Hypothesis without a provider in the programme: the fixed-point property for trees with finite edge stabilizers holds for finitely generated groups with one end (Bowditch, Lemma 6.6; needs groups acting on trees and ends of groups).

Hypothesis without a provider in the programme: a finitely presented one-ended group without elements of finite order that does not split over a finite or two-ended subgroup, acting as a minimal convergence group on a dendrite, fixes a point of it; indeed the dendrite is a point (Bowditch, Connectedness properties of limit sets, Lemma 1.4; needs real trees: Levitt's theorem on non-nesting actions and the Bestvina-Feighn theorem on stable actions).

Not proved in the course: Theorem 6.1 of Bowditch for groups that have infinite subgroups without elements of infinite order. Original statement: a one-ended finitely generated group with a minimal convergence action on a continuum M; if M has a cut point which is not a parabolic fixed point (stabilizer infinite without loxodromic elements), then D(M) is not a point. Missing step: an infinite edge stabilizer in the trees of the induction must be shown to contain an element of infinite order, or the argument must be done for infinite torsion stabilizers.
Not in the course: the equivalence of the definition by sequences with proper discontinuity on distinct triples.
free_sources: B. H. Bowditch, Treelike structures arising from continua and convergence groups (author's version of Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 662, 1999), Section 6
